conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. You’re here because of worsening abdominal pain after your trip. Can you tell me more about what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. I was on vacation and had mild pain, but it got much worse when I flew back. I started vomiting, couldn’t keep anything down, and had sharp pain in my upper belly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned one episode of bloody diarrhea, followed by pale stools. That’s concerning for a flare of your pancreatitis. You’ve had this before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s usually linked to my vasculitis. I’ve had flares from stress or certain foods, but I’m not sure what triggered this one.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Your labs came back — lipase is normal, which is unusual for acute pancreatitis, but given your history, we’re treating this as an acute flare on top of chronic pancreatitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not showing up in the blood test, but you still think it’s pancreatitis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. In chronic cases like yours, especially with prior surgery, the enzymes don’t always rise. Your symptoms and history are very consistent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. My boyfriend was diagnosed with shigella and campylobacter — could that be part of this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We considered that. You started azithromycin from your PCP, so we kept you on it initially just in case. But you only had one bloody stool, no fever, and no other signs of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given the low likelihood, we’re going to stop the antibiotic. We don’t want to risk side effects if it’s not needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I was worried about spreading it or making things worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Totally understandable, but you’re not showing signs of active infection. We’ll monitor, but for now, we’re focusing on your pain and pancreas flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve also noticed redness on my face, arms, and belly. Could that be my vasculitis acting up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s very possible. We’re continuing your methotrexate and hydroxychloroquine to manage that. You’re due for your weekly methotrexate shot — we’ll give that tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been on it for a while and it helps with the malabsorption too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right, and we’ll keep your pancreatic enzyme supplements — those five capsules with meals — to help digestion while your pancreas is inflamed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pain? It’s still pretty bad, even after the IV meds in the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re giving IV fluids and starting IV hydromorphone for now. Once your pain settles, we’ll switch to oral meds. We need to keep your stomach at rest, so no food yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long will I be on IVs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Usually a day or two. We’ll start with clear liquids once your pain improves and you’re not vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your pain is a bit better today, right? We’re going to try advancing your diet to clear liquids if you’re up for it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the pain’s more manageable. Can I have water or broth?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. We’ll start slow — sips of water, then broth. If you tolerate it, we’ll move to full liquids tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. I’m also feeling bloated — is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the X-ray showed significant constipation. We’re adding senna and docusate to help — especially since pain meds can make it worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll take those. And I got my methotrexate shot this morning?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it was given earlier. We’ll continue your other usual meds — omeprazole for reflux, betaxolol and fludrocortisone for your tachycardia, and your anxiety meds as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well — kept down apple juice and broth. We’re upgrading to a full liquid diet: milk, pudding, things like that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds good. Can I go home tomorrow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you keep tolerating liquids and your pain stays controlled with oral meds, yes — likely discharge tomorrow or the day after.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. You made it through the night without vomiting and your pain is down to a 2 out of 10. That’s great progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much better. Can I eat real food now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll try a light meal — maybe toast and applesauce. If that goes well, you can go home this afternoon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did great with lunch — no nausea or pain increase. We’re going to prepare for discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the azithromycin I was taking?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can stop it. We don’t think you have a bacterial infection. No need to continue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home with oral hydromorphone — one every four hours as needed. Don’t drive or operate machinery while taking it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And the senna and docusate?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep them while on the narcotic. Stop if you develop diarrhea. Otherwise, continue your usual meds — enzymes, omeprazole, methotrexate, etc.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll follow up with my rheumatologist and GI doctor?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and call your PCP if you have fever, worsening pain, or can’t keep fluids down. Otherwise, you’re doing really well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check before discharge. You’re stable, tolerating food, and pain is well-controlled. Ready to go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, thank you. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember: no azithromycin, take pain meds only as needed, and follow up with your doctors. Take care.
